BOW.Quote: Helpers may aid the breeding pair in raising young (Brackbill 1970b, Tarbell 1983). At one nest, the helper was one of the previous year's offspring of the adult female and a different male (Brackbill 1970b). In another case, the helper was the offspring of the breeding pair from a previous season (Tarbell 1983). Such helping behavior is unusual for parids and has only been reported in two other species, Bridled Titmice (Baeolophus wollweberi; Nocedal and Ficken 1998a) and Black Tits (Parus niger; Brown 1987). There is no information on whether helping affects breeding success of the adult pair.

BOW.Quote: At 25 Vermont nests observed by videography, one female fed at each nest, with two provisioning males most common (60%), followed by nests with one provisioning male (20%), nests with three males (16%), and nests with four males (4%; VCE). Four males documented to feed at >1 nest within single breeding season, and three males fed two broods simultaneously (nests 186–443 m apart). One male simultaneously provisioned at two nests 443 m apart, shared feeding of nestlings at first nest, was sole male feeder at second nest. First nest fledged 3 d after second nest hatched; male then left care of fledglings to the other male and fed second brood at nearly twice the rate as he had fed young at first nest. Individual female, total male, and total adult provisioning rates did not differ between nests with single and multiple male feeders. The number of male feeders was negatively correlated to prey abundance on female home ranges, suggesting that females might balance the cost of low prey abundance by copulating with multiple males and attracting male feeders (Strong et al. 2004). Overall, females fed nestlings at more than twice the rate of males (Goetz et al 2003). Male feeding rates increased with nestling age until day 7–8 and then decreased until fledging. Some males did not feed at nests in which they sired young, and some males fed at nests in which they sired no young (Goetz et al. 2003). Multiple male feeders also reported at nests in Quebec (Y. Aubry) and New Brunswick (Askanas 2012). In highlands of New Brunswick, 78% of nests had two or more male feeders (Askanas 2012). BOW.Quote: Although White-rumped Shama is not reported to be a cooperative breeding species, helping behavior was observed at 2 out of 32 nests on O‘ahu I. (8). In each case, 2 different adult males were observed feeding nestlings of a single female. At one of these nests, 2 males fed the single nestling at 1, 9, 10, and 12 d after hatching; the males did not behave aggressively toward one another. At the other nest, a second male was observed on a single day; it fed the nestlings 3 times but was attacked repeatedly by resident male. Unknown whether these males were reproductively inactive helpers, or if they sired some of the nestlings through extra-pair copulations or polyandrous matings.

BOW.Quote: Nests often attract the attention of extra adults that associate with a pair for up to an entire breeding season; these extra birds are sometimes tolerated and occasionally lead to polygyny (217). In New York, extra birds were predominantly males (219, 325), whereas in Washington, extra birds were yearling females (217). Extra adults contribute relatively little to feeding young, but they are known to mob predators and assist in nest-building, incubation, and brooding young (219, 325, 217). Extra adults may be using nest attendance as a breeding strategy either to replace one pair member should something happen to it (217) or to commit sexually selected infanticide (219, 325), providing an opportunity for males to take over the breeding female (see Behavior: Sexual Behavior). Nests that are attended by helpers often are ones occupied by older females (325), consistent with the interpretation that male attendants are trying to secure high-quality females as mates.

BOW.Quote: Although ca. 20% of Canada Jay pairs studied in Quebec and Ontario have an associated nonbreeder on their territories at the onset of breeding and ca. 65% of these are the pair's own offspring from the previous breeding season, the nonbreeders do not feed the current year's nestlings and the breeders energetically drive them away if they approach the nest. Starting immediately after the nestlings fledge, however, adults relax this vigilance and on intensively observed territories in Ontario and Quebec some non-breeders have accounted for over 30% of all observed feedings of the young (189, 190). Proposed explanation for this pattern holds that, compared to other jays, Canada Jays are particularly vulnerable to nest predators because they have poorer defensive abilities (being smaller and generally having only one extra group member, if any). In such a species, suppression of allofeeding, along with a smaller than expected clutch size and a very low provisioning rate by the adults (achieved by bringing largest possible loads at the consequently minimum possible frequency), may reduce predator-attracting visits to the nest and thus contribute to higher breeding success (166, 191). BOW.Quote: Polygynandrous mating system, 2–5 males share large overlapping ranges of 2–5 females, group ranges (9–38 ha) more or less exclusive; males compete to mate with fertile females, females compete to attract males; solicitation display by female, which has high copulation rate (up to 1000 per clutch), usually involving several males. Five breeding groups studied in a Swiss alpine region each consisted of 1–4 females with exclusive territories, and 3–5 males which co-operated in defending group territory; within group, linear dominance relationship usually well established among alpha, beta and subordinate males, both frequent copulation and mate-guarding strategies being used, and females advertised their fertility, solicited most of copulations and mated many times with several males (c. 350 matings during short fertile period of ten days), while intensity of mate-guarding and copulation frequency were highest on day preceding and throughout laying period; in this polygynandrous system, females of studied population lacked full male help but might have benefited from greater genetic variation of their offspring, while males varied widely in lifetime reproductive success, higher-ranking males raising their fitness to above average (4). Nest, built by female, a cup made from grass, moss and plant stems, lined with hair and feathers, sited in rock crevice or beneath rock or grass tussock on cliff or shallower slope. Clutch 3–4 eggs; incubation by female, period 11–15 days; chicksphoto fed by both sexes, but contribution of each male varies; of 38 broods studied in Pyrenees, 5% fed by female alone, 68% by female and one male, 24% by female and two males, 3% by female and three males; male care influenced by share of matings, hence paternity

BOW.Quote: In contrast to Western Bluebirds, Eastern Bluebirds rarely have helpers. In joint nesting, 2 females lay 2 clutches of eggs synchronously in the same nest, then incubate synchronously and sequentially, and cooperate with a male in feeding nestlings and fledglings. In S. Carolina, 5 of 4,299 nesting attempts in field seasons 1977‚Äì1991 were joint nesting ventures; 2 of these 5 attempts were by the same previously known and banded females, so it was reliably inferred that these jointly-nesting females were mother and daughter (PAG, JHP). Juvenile helpers are rare; almost all reports are of juveniles entering nesting cavities when adults are feeding later broods (Pinkowski 1975d)‚Äîsomething documented on video films twice by PAG and JHP. Adult helpers seen occasionally and irregularly (Pinkowski 1976d, PAG), usually second-year son of current breeders.

BOW.Quote: Extremely rare if not absent in most temperate populations. One report from California of a juvenile from a first brood helping its father (and possibly mother; she was unmarked) feed young of a second brood in the same season (275. Second report from Kansas of a juvenile of unknown origin feeding young and removing a fecal sac from a nest at least one time (Timson and Farley 2003). Helpers-at-the-nest also reported in Costa Rica, but not in all nests and such behavior was apparently rare (Skutch 1940, 176, Skutch 1983, Winnett-Murray 1986). Skutch (1983) speculated helping was more likely when young from a previous brood sleep with the mother in the nest while she incubates in a subsequent breeding attempt. In one case in Costa Rica, an individual known not to be the offspring of a resident parents' previous brood attempted to feed young; parents repeatedly attacked that individual (Winnett-Murray 1986: 23).

BOW.Quote: Does not occur (17, MTM). Trios of adults occasionally form, but are rarely stable; a trio in New York remained together from early in nestling period to > 1 mo after young had fledged (MTM). The fate of the third bird in next year was determined in 2 of 3 cases in which the third bird was banded and sex determined. In one case, a female returned to breed on territory where she was seen in previous year (former male and female occupants of territory failed to return). In the other case, a male established residence on adjacent territory in following year. Third birds in trios probably represent birds prospecting for a breeding site in the next year. One case of incest is known: an experienced female (> 9 yr old) bred with a son raised in previous year (MTM).  Smith, W. J. (1966d). Communication and relationships in the genus Tyrannus.
